source: Voltage equals current times resistance: V = IR.
Students think a resistor's resistance changes when the current through it changes.

Push harder and more current flows; put something in the way and less flows. The "something in the way" is resistance. A bulb filament or a resistor resists the flow, turning electrical energy into heat and light. Solving the law is a one-step equation, in any complete circuit.
Ohm's law: $$\role{voltage}{V} = \role{current}{I}\,\role{resistance}{R}$$ Voltage (V) = current (A) × resistance in ohms (Ω). So $I = \dfrac{V}{R}$ and $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$.

For many materials, doubling the voltage doubles the current: current and voltage are proportional. The resistance is the constant ratio $\dfrac{V}{I}$, a property of the resistor itself, set by its material, length and thickness. A thin, long wire has more resistance than a short, thick one, just as a narrow pipe lets less water through.

A 12 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor. Find the current.
A lamp draws 0.5 A from a 6 V supply. What is its resistance?

Thinking a resistor's resistance changes when the current through it changes. For an ordinary resistor, if you double the voltage, the current doubles too, and $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$ stays the same. Resistance depends on the resistor, not on what you connect it to. (A bulb filament is an exception in one way: its resistance rises as it heats up.)
